medical.title: Understudied gut fungus may help repair radiation-damaged DNA and limit intestinal injury
medical.summary: The gut microbiome has been a popular topic for a while now, but the focus is usually on good bacteria. A new study, published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, suggests that we may want to pay attention to the fungi in our guts as well. The study examined the effects of radiation on mice, comparing mice inoculated with a filamentous fungus called Mucor racemosus with a control group, and found that M. racemosus facilitated processes that protected the mice from radiation damage.

medical.title: Inside the brain: Rethinking the mechanisms of Alzheimer's disease
medical.summary: Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia. For many years, researchers believed that its main cause was a buildup of toxic proteins. But recent findings suggest that the problem may have another origin, specifically in the bloodstream.

medical.title: Body size cannot tell you how fit someone is, but it shapes how people are judged
medical.summary: U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has been criticized after sharing a photograph of two people in uniform from a Canadian youth cadet program with the caption "this is real." The image showed a teenage cadet receiving a medal from someone reported to be a volunteer instructor.

medical.title: How losing the 'guardian of the genome' can damage DNA and drive cancer
medical.summary: A new study finds that when p53, one of the most important cancer-protecting genes, stops working, cells produce too much RNA and consume excessive amounts of the building blocks needed to copy their DNA. This shortage disrupts DNA replication, leading to DNA damage, chromosomal instability and major genetic changes that can promote cancer development.

medical.title: Brain's inhibitory circuits emerge as a potential brake on adult glioma progression
medical.summary: Brain tumors do not grow in isolation. They develop within the highly active environment of the brain, where neurons continuously exchange electrical and chemical signals. While previous studies have shown that neuronal activity can promote glioma growth, a new study published in Neuron reveals that some brain circuits can have the opposite effect: They can act as a brake on tumor progression.

medical.title: Newly discovered stem cell reveals potential drug target for spinal stenosis
medical.summary: Researchers at Weill Cornell Medicine and Hospital for Special Surgery have discovered the unspecialized stem cells that give rise to the body's tendons and ligaments, the tissues connecting muscles and bones.

medical.title: Trial: Prostate cancer fitness cuts treatment side effects
medical.summary: Findings from STAMINA, the largest trial of its kind, published in The Lancet Oncology, show that a purpose-designed lifestyle program offering structured exercise, dietary advice and behavioral support as part of routine cancer care reduced deterioration in quality of life in men undergoing treatment for prostate cancer by up to one-third.

medical.title: Scientists in China discover new tick-borne virus that causes flu-like illness
medical.summary: Scientists in China have identified a novel tick-borne virus that causes an influenza-like illness characterized by fever, fatigue, gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms and abnormal lab findings. The team, led by researchers from the State Key Laboratory of Pathogen and Biosecurity in Beijing, has designated the new orthonairovirus as the Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV).

medical.title: A single IV treatment retrains immune cells to fight autoimmune diseases in early trial
medical.summary: CAR T-cell therapy is an immune-reprogramming procedure that turns a patient's own immune cells into cancer-fighting specialists. The entire process is complex, but researchers have now found a faster way to achieve similar effects using a single intravenous (IV) drip of a harmless engineered virus.

medical.title: Weight loss surgery can improve reproductive health of women living with obesity
medical.summary: Metabolic bariatric surgery improves menstrual cycle frequency and symptoms of polycystic ovaries in women living with obesity, a new study from the University of Surrey reports.

medical.title: Does 'R U OK? Day' actually improve people's mental health?
medical.summary: Every September, Australians are encouraged to ask someone a simple question: "Are you OK?"

medical.title: Pigmentation measurement could improve laser safety standards across skin tones
medical.summary: Lasers are used in a growing number of medical and imaging applications, from surgery to photoacoustic imaging. To protect patients, safety guidelines define the maximum amount of laser energy that can be delivered to the skin without causing injury. However, these limits do not account for differences in skin pigmentation.

medical.title: Money problems may age your brain faster
medical.summary: Persistent financial hardship in early and middle adulthood was linked to poorer thinking skills by the 50s and more signs of brain aging later in life. Researchers say years of chronic stress and financial worry may gradually take a toll on the brain.

medical.title: Alzheimer’s may leave a mark on the brain long before plaques appear
medical.summary: Brain changes associated with Alzheimer’s may begin at least seven years before amyloid plaques become detectable with current PET scans. Researchers uncovered the signal by tracking healthy older adults with repeated brain imaging over nearly 20 years. The discovery could help scientists identify Alzheimer’s earlier and suggests that important disease processes may start before visible plaque buildup.

medical.title: What Brazil’s supercentenarians can teach us about living to 120
medical.summary: Why does Brazil have so many supercentenarians? Researchers are trying to find out – and the early findings are in The post What Brazil’s supercentenarians can teach us about living to 120 appeared first on Positive News .

science.title: Tiny polymer particles keep water jets stable for longer
science.summary: Tiny, soft polymer particles—known as microgels—can help to stabilize extremely thin liquid jets. How this works is the finding of a study led by researchers at TU Darmstadt, which has been published in Nature Communications. The findings could be of interest for the development of needle-free medical injection systems.

science.title: The DESI legacy imaging survey releases the largest 2D map of the universe
science.summary: In 2012, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) was commissioned to measure the effect of dark energy, the mysterious force driving the expansion of the cosmos. Since then, the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys have obtained optical images of tens of millions of galaxies and quasars, including through NOIRLab's Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO). In recent news, the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys team made its 11th data release (DR 11), constituting the largest-ever 2D map of the universe.

science.title: A vital native bee highway can start in your own backyard
science.summary: When it comes to bees, most of us can identify the ubiquitous honey bee (Apis mellifera) and that's about it.

science.title: How 'hyperselection' is making modern life efficient, pleasant—and boring
science.summary: It's difficult to imagine a song like Queen's 1975 "Bohemian Rhapsody" topping the charts today. Almost six minutes long, it moves through several radically different musical sections and famously ignores the conventional structure of a pop song. It seems almost designed to break the rules of what a hit single should be.

science.title: Two-color X-ray pulses capture the same nanoparticle at two moments in time
science.summary: One big dream of ultrafast science has been to watch changes in nanoparticles or biomolecules on their natural timescale. Experimentally, this can be realized by taking two snapshots of the same object only femtoseconds apart. However, no detector is fast enough to record the two snapshots separately—they end up on top of each other in a single image.

science.title: We teach students how to argue. But are we teaching them how to listen?
science.summary: Picture a senior English classroom.

science.title: Reconstructed ancient protein maps how bacterial enzymes evolved distinct functions
science.summary: How do related proteins develop different functions? This is the question investigated by a research team involving Kiel University, DESY and the Center for Structural Systems Biology (CSSB). Led by Holger Sondermann, professor at Kiel University and head of the Structural Microbiology group at DESY, the researchers reconstructed the common ancestor of two bacterial enzymes and produced the long-extinct protein in the laboratory.

science.title: New digital tool shows exactly where California's water goes—and how climate change might disrupt it
science.summary: Water has always been one of California's most contested resources. For more than a century, battles have raged over how much of the state's water should be diverted to farmland, pumped into cities or used to conserve aquatic ecosystems—and at times, these clashes have even led to violence. The state's water system consists of a dizzying array of reservoirs, rivers, dams and aqueducts, making it challenging even for experts to understand the trade-offs of different management decisions.

science.title: New blending method gives common polymers a visible, reversible stress signal
science.summary: Polymeric materials, such as plastics and rubbers, are essential in everyday life. However, detecting where mechanical stress is concentrated inside them remains a challenge.

science.title: What happens when you flush? Study reveals how toilet aerosols reach the breathing zone
science.summary: Researchers from Flinders University have found that flushing toilets can release aerosols and bioaerosols into the surrounding air, with some studies detecting particles at heights corresponding to adults' breathing zones.

science.title: Genomic analysis clarifies origin of unusual tail in endangered Tsushima leopard cat
science.summary: Tsushima leopard cats are an endangered species found only on this isolated island. The most recent government survey estimated the population at around 150 individuals, and because domestic cats also inhabit the same landscape, introgression is a legitimate conservation concern.

science.title: Isle of Jura research casts new light on how rivers carve through landscapes
science.summary: The waters of the remote Scottish island of Jura have long been famous for making whiskey. Now, the island's rivers have helped geologists learn more about how rivers erode rocks, providing new evidence that what streams carry plays an important role in how they carve through landscapes.

science.title: Rare pulsar unleashes 114 giant pulses in a single hour
science.summary: Astronomers have detected extreme, never-before-seen behavior from a rare kind of pulsar and stumbled on a surprising link to one of astronomy's biggest current mysteries. Using 174 hours of radio observations, researchers detected PSR J1227-4853, a rapidly spinning neutron star known as a "transitional millisecond pulsar," which unleashes hundreds of ultrashort, ultrapowerful "giant pulses." Their paper was published in The Astrophysical Journal on July 31.

science.title: Investments promising social or environmental benefits need tougher anti‑greenwashing rules
science.summary: Investment funds increasingly promise to deliver social or environmental benefits alongside financial returns. Regulators rightly ask whether these "impact investment" claims are accurate.

science.title: Dog parks are an antidote to the isolation and divisions that social media can fuel
science.summary: The case against social media has become so well rehearsed that most people can easily merge it into ordinary conversation: It makes people lonely. It sorts them into camps. It hands them a room full of people who already agree with them and calls that a community.

science.title: Decades-old museum specimens reveal 10 extraordinary new worms
science.summary: Scientists have discovered that one of the most unusual creatures in the animal kingdom is far more diverse and evolutionarily complex than previously known. An international team led by the University of Göttingen has reconstructed the evolutionary history of branching marine worms—rare annelids that live hidden inside sea sponges and whose bodies branch repeatedly into multiple posterior ends.

science.title: Do black holes have hidden hair? Scientists find a new way to check
science.summary: When two black holes crash together and merge, the newly formed black hole rings like a bell, sending out gravitational waves with specific frequencies that fade over time. This brief, fading pattern of waves is called ringdown, and it may hold secrets about what is hiding around black holes.

science.title: Behind the scenes: The science that confirmed Australia's first H5 bird flu case
science.summary: When a suspected case of H5 bird flu arrived in Australia, CSIRO scientists knew the first hours would matter.

science.title: How researchers are helping Canada understand a changing climate
science.summary: More than two dozen University of Victoria researchers contributed to "Canada's Changing Climate Report 2026," the country's most comprehensive assessment of how climate change is affecting communities, ecosystems and coastlines across Canada.

science.title: White paper suggests 5 ways K–12 leaders can strengthen teacher recognition beyond appreciation weeks
science.summary: University of Phoenix College of Doctoral Studies has published a new white paper, "Beyond Appreciation Weeks: Building Teacher Recognition Into the Everyday Work of K–12 Leadership," by Contessa Walker-Jackson, Ed.D., alumni fellow with the University's Center for Educational and Instructional Technology Research (CEITR).

science.title: One quarter of Australian kids are 'developmentally vulnerable' when they start school
science.summary: We know the first five years are a crucial time in a child's life. Early experiences, such as family relationships or exposure to trauma, shape brain architecture, which lays the foundation for children's learning, behavior and health.

science.title: Feeling angry? Don't blow off steam. Try these tips instead
science.summary: After a bad night's sleep, you squabble with your kids at breakfast. Then a neighbor blocks you in. When you finally get to work an hour late, your boss makes one more impossible demand. No wonder you're angry with the world.

science.title: The 20th data release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey
science.summary: The Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), the largest multispectral imaging and spectroscopic redshift survey of the cosmos, has released its 20th data release (DR 20). It is also the third release of the survey's fifth phase (SDSS-V), representing a massive operational expansion of the legacy established with prior releases. This milestone provides an unprecedented look at the stars, the interstellar medium (ISM) and distant galaxies that make up the cosmos.

science.title: Three quantum phases in chromium-based material hint at a spin-triplet superconductor
science.summary: Superconductors are materials that conduct electricity without electrical resistance when cooled below a specific critical temperature. These materials have proved promising for the development of various technologies, including medical imaging instruments, particle accelerators, ultrasensitive detectors and quantum processors.

science.title: Interstellar solar sails hit a strange problem at 75% of light speed
science.summary: Solar sails pushed by powerful lasers could reach incredible speeds, but relativity may eventually make the light itself work against them. At around 75% of the speed of light, scattered photons can begin creating drag, adding a surprising obstacle to interstellar travel.

environment.title: Marine conservation collides with mining in Indonesia’s biodiversity-rich Moramo Bay
environment.summary: SOUTH KONAWE, Indonesia — A marine protected area in Indonesia’s Southeast Sulawesi province is home to a critically depleted population of humphead wrasse. The species presence helped the area gain its protected status, but mining permits overlap parts of the conservation zone and line its coast. environment.title: Galaxy Gallery: Galactic Gems Glisten in New Gallery From NASA’s Chandra
environment.summary: This gallery displays a collection of 16 galactic images from Chandra and other telescopes. Astronomers put galaxies into three main categories: spirals like our own Milky Way, ellipticals that are older and likely the results of mergers, and irregulars that can encompass a wide range of galactic phenomena. All types are represented in this collection. Each galactic image contains X-ray data from Chandra combined with data from telescopes such as NASA’s Webb, Hubble, IXPE, Swift, and NuSTAR, and others both in space and on the ground. The post Galaxy Gallery: Galactic Gems Glisten in New Gallery From NASA’s Chandra appeared first on NASA Science .

environment.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
environment.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

environment.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
environment.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

environment.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
environment.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

environment.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
environment.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

mix_items.title: Tiny polymer particles keep water jets stable for longer
mix_items.summary: Tiny, soft polymer particles—known as microgels—can help to stabilize extremely thin liquid jets. How this works is the finding of a study led by researchers at TU Darmstadt, which has been published in Nature Communications. The findings could be of interest for the development of needle-free medical injection systems.

mix_items.title: The DESI legacy imaging survey releases the largest 2D map of the universe
mix_items.summary: In 2012, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) was commissioned to measure the effect of dark energy, the mysterious force driving the expansion of the cosmos. Since then, the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys have obtained optical images of tens of millions of galaxies and quasars, including through NOIRLab's Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO). In recent news, the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys team made its 11th data release (DR 11), constituting the largest-ever 2D map of the universe.

mix_items.title: Understudied gut fungus may help repair radiation-damaged DNA and limit intestinal injury
mix_items.summary: The gut microbiome has been a popular topic for a while now, but the focus is usually on good bacteria. A new study, published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, suggests that we may want to pay attention to the fungi in our guts as well. The study examined the effects of radiation on mice, comparing mice inoculated with a filamentous fungus called Mucor racemosus with a control group, and found that M. racemosus facilitated processes that protected the mice from radiation damage.

mix_items.title: Inside the brain: Rethinking the mechanisms of Alzheimer's disease
mix_items.summary: Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia. For many years, researchers believed that its main cause was a buildup of toxic proteins. But recent findings suggest that the problem may have another origin, specifically in the bloodstream.

mix_items.title: Body size cannot tell you how fit someone is, but it shapes how people are judged
mix_items.summary: U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has been criticized after sharing a photograph of two people in uniform from a Canadian youth cadet program with the caption "this is real." The image showed a teenage cadet receiving a medal from someone reported to be a volunteer instructor.

mix_items.title: A vital native bee highway can start in your own backyard
mix_items.summary: When it comes to bees, most of us can identify the ubiquitous honey bee (Apis mellifera) and that's about it.

mix_items.title: How 'hyperselection' is making modern life efficient, pleasant—and boring
mix_items.summary: It's difficult to imagine a song like Queen's 1975 "Bohemian Rhapsody" topping the charts today. Almost six minutes long, it moves through several radically different musical sections and famously ignores the conventional structure of a pop song. It seems almost designed to break the rules of what a hit single should be.

mix_items.title: How losing the 'guardian of the genome' can damage DNA and drive cancer
mix_items.summary: A new study finds that when p53, one of the most important cancer-protecting genes, stops working, cells produce too much RNA and consume excessive amounts of the building blocks needed to copy their DNA. This shortage disrupts DNA replication, leading to DNA damage, chromosomal instability and major genetic changes that can promote cancer development.

mix_items.title: Two-color X-ray pulses capture the same nanoparticle at two moments in time
mix_items.summary: One big dream of ultrafast science has been to watch changes in nanoparticles or biomolecules on their natural timescale. Experimentally, this can be realized by taking two snapshots of the same object only femtoseconds apart. However, no detector is fast enough to record the two snapshots separately—they end up on top of each other in a single image.

mix_items.title: Brain's inhibitory circuits emerge as a potential brake on adult glioma progression
mix_items.summary: Brain tumors do not grow in isolation. They develop within the highly active environment of the brain, where neurons continuously exchange electrical and chemical signals. While previous studies have shown that neuronal activity can promote glioma growth, a new study published in Neuron reveals that some brain circuits can have the opposite effect: They can act as a brake on tumor progression.

mix_items.title: Newly discovered stem cell reveals potential drug target for spinal stenosis
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Weill Cornell Medicine and Hospital for Special Surgery have discovered the unspecialized stem cells that give rise to the body's tendons and ligaments, the tissues connecting muscles and bones.

mix_items.title: We teach students how to argue. But are we teaching them how to listen?
mix_items.summary: Picture a senior English classroom.

mix_items.title: Reconstructed ancient protein maps how bacterial enzymes evolved distinct functions
mix_items.summary: How do related proteins develop different functions? This is the question investigated by a research team involving Kiel University, DESY and the Center for Structural Systems Biology (CSSB). Led by Holger Sondermann, professor at Kiel University and head of the Structural Microbiology group at DESY, the researchers reconstructed the common ancestor of two bacterial enzymes and produced the long-extinct protein in the laboratory.

mix_items.title: New digital tool shows exactly where California's water goes—and how climate change might disrupt it
mix_items.summary: Water has always been one of California's most contested resources. For more than a century, battles have raged over how much of the state's water should be diverted to farmland, pumped into cities or used to conserve aquatic ecosystems—and at times, these clashes have even led to violence. The state's water system consists of a dizzying array of reservoirs, rivers, dams and aqueducts, making it challenging even for experts to understand the trade-offs of different management decisions.

mix_items.title: New blending method gives common polymers a visible, reversible stress signal
mix_items.summary: Polymeric materials, such as plastics and rubbers, are essential in everyday life. However, detecting where mechanical stress is concentrated inside them remains a challenge.

mix_items.title: What happens when you flush? Study reveals how toilet aerosols reach the breathing zone
mix_items.summary: Researchers from Flinders University have found that flushing toilets can release aerosols and bioaerosols into the surrounding air, with some studies detecting particles at heights corresponding to adults' breathing zones.

mix_items.title: Genomic analysis clarifies origin of unusual tail in endangered Tsushima leopard cat
mix_items.summary: Tsushima leopard cats are an endangered species found only on this isolated island. The most recent government survey estimated the population at around 150 individuals, and because domestic cats also inhabit the same landscape, introgression is a legitimate conservation concern.

mix_items.title: Isle of Jura research casts new light on how rivers carve through landscapes
mix_items.summary: The waters of the remote Scottish island of Jura have long been famous for making whiskey. Now, the island's rivers have helped geologists learn more about how rivers erode rocks, providing new evidence that what streams carry plays an important role in how they carve through landscapes.

mix_items.title: Trial: Prostate cancer fitness cuts treatment side effects
mix_items.summary: Findings from STAMINA, the largest trial of its kind, published in The Lancet Oncology, show that a purpose-designed lifestyle program offering structured exercise, dietary advice and behavioral support as part of routine cancer care reduced deterioration in quality of life in men undergoing treatment for prostate cancer by up to one-third.

mix_items.title: Scientists in China discover new tick-borne virus that causes flu-like illness
mix_items.summary: Scientists in China have identified a novel tick-borne virus that causes an influenza-like illness characterized by fever, fatigue, gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms and abnormal lab findings. The team, led by researchers from the State Key Laboratory of Pathogen and Biosecurity in Beijing, has designated the new orthonairovirus as the Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV).

mix_items.title: Rare pulsar unleashes 114 giant pulses in a single hour
mix_items.summary: Astronomers have detected extreme, never-before-seen behavior from a rare kind of pulsar and stumbled on a surprising link to one of astronomy's biggest current mysteries. Using 174 hours of radio observations, researchers detected PSR J1227-4853, a rapidly spinning neutron star known as a "transitional millisecond pulsar," which unleashes hundreds of ultrashort, ultrapowerful "giant pulses." Their paper was published in The Astrophysical Journal on July 31.

mix_items.title: Investments promising social or environmental benefits need tougher anti‑greenwashing rules
mix_items.summary: Investment funds increasingly promise to deliver social or environmental benefits alongside financial returns. Regulators rightly ask whether these "impact investment" claims are accurate.

mix_items.title: A single IV treatment retrains immune cells to fight autoimmune diseases in early trial
mix_items.summary: CAR T-cell therapy is an immune-reprogramming procedure that turns a patient's own immune cells into cancer-fighting specialists. The entire process is complex, but researchers have now found a faster way to achieve similar effects using a single intravenous (IV) drip of a harmless engineered virus.

mix_items.title: Dog parks are an antidote to the isolation and divisions that social media can fuel
mix_items.summary: The case against social media has become so well rehearsed that most people can easily merge it into ordinary conversation: It makes people lonely. It sorts them into camps. It hands them a room full of people who already agree with them and calls that a community.

mix_items.title: Decades-old museum specimens reveal 10 extraordinary new worms
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that one of the most unusual creatures in the animal kingdom is far more diverse and evolutionarily complex than previously known. An international team led by the University of Göttingen has reconstructed the evolutionary history of branching marine worms—rare annelids that live hidden inside sea sponges and whose bodies branch repeatedly into multiple posterior ends.

mix_items.title: Do black holes have hidden hair? Scientists find a new way to check
mix_items.summary: When two black holes crash together and merge, the newly formed black hole rings like a bell, sending out gravitational waves with specific frequencies that fade over time. This brief, fading pattern of waves is called ringdown, and it may hold secrets about what is hiding around black holes.

mix_items.title: Weight loss surgery can improve reproductive health of women living with obesity
mix_items.summary: Metabolic bariatric surgery improves menstrual cycle frequency and symptoms of polycystic ovaries in women living with obesity, a new study from the University of Surrey reports.

mix_items.title: Behind the scenes: The science that confirmed Australia's first H5 bird flu case
mix_items.summary: When a suspected case of H5 bird flu arrived in Australia, CSIRO scientists knew the first hours would matter.

mix_items.title: How researchers are helping Canada understand a changing climate
mix_items.summary: More than two dozen University of Victoria researchers contributed to "Canada's Changing Climate Report 2026," the country's most comprehensive assessment of how climate change is affecting communities, ecosystems and coastlines across Canada.

mix_items.title: White paper suggests 5 ways K–12 leaders can strengthen teacher recognition beyond appreciation weeks
mix_items.summary: University of Phoenix College of Doctoral Studies has published a new white paper, "Beyond Appreciation Weeks: Building Teacher Recognition Into the Everyday Work of K–12 Leadership," by Contessa Walker-Jackson, Ed.D., alumni fellow with the University's Center for Educational and Instructional Technology Research (CEITR).

mix_items.title: One quarter of Australian kids are 'developmentally vulnerable' when they start school
mix_items.summary: We know the first five years are a crucial time in a child's life. Early experiences, such as family relationships or exposure to trauma, shape brain architecture, which lays the foundation for children's learning, behavior and health.

mix_items.title: Does 'R U OK? Day' actually improve people's mental health?
mix_items.summary: Every September, Australians are encouraged to ask someone a simple question: "Are you OK?"

mix_items.title: Feeling angry? Don't blow off steam. Try these tips instead
mix_items.summary: After a bad night's sleep, you squabble with your kids at breakfast. Then a neighbor blocks you in. When you finally get to work an hour late, your boss makes one more impossible demand. No wonder you're angry with the world.

mix_items.title: The 20th data release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey
mix_items.summary: The Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), the largest multispectral imaging and spectroscopic redshift survey of the cosmos, has released its 20th data release (DR 20). It is also the third release of the survey's fifth phase (SDSS-V), representing a massive operational expansion of the legacy established with prior releases. This milestone provides an unprecedented look at the stars, the interstellar medium (ISM) and distant galaxies that make up the cosmos.

mix_items.title: Pigmentation measurement could improve laser safety standards across skin tones
mix_items.summary: Lasers are used in a growing number of medical and imaging applications, from surgery to photoacoustic imaging. To protect patients, safety guidelines define the maximum amount of laser energy that can be delivered to the skin without causing injury. However, these limits do not account for differences in skin pigmentation.

mix_items.title: Three quantum phases in chromium-based material hint at a spin-triplet superconductor
mix_items.summary: Superconductors are materials that conduct electricity without electrical resistance when cooled below a specific critical temperature. These materials have proved promising for the development of various technologies, including medical imaging instruments, particle accelerators, ultrasensitive detectors and quantum processors.

mix_items.title: Marine conservation collides with mining in Indonesia’s biodiversity-rich Moramo Bay
mix_items.summary: SOUTH KONAWE, Indonesia — A marine protected area in Indonesia’s Southeast Sulawesi province is home to a critically depleted population of humphead wrasse. The species presence helped the area gain its protected status, but mining permits overlap parts of the conservation zone and line its coast. A 2024 government survey, published the following year, found […]

mix_items.title: Interstellar solar sails hit a strange problem at 75% of light speed
mix_items.summary: Solar sails pushed by powerful lasers could reach incredible speeds, but relativity may eventually make the light itself work against them. At around 75% of the speed of light, scattered photons can begin creating drag, adding a surprising obstacle to interstellar travel.

mix_items.title: Money problems may age your brain faster
mix_items.summary: Persistent financial hardship in early and middle adulthood was linked to poorer thinking skills by the 50s and more signs of brain aging later in life. Researchers say years of chronic stress and financial worry may gradually take a toll on the brain.

mix_items.title: Alzheimer’s may leave a mark on the brain long before plaques appear
mix_items.summary: Brain changes associated with Alzheimer’s may begin at least seven years before amyloid plaques become detectable with current PET scans. Researchers uncovered the signal by tracking healthy older adults with repeated brain imaging over nearly 20 years. The discovery could help scientists identify Alzheimer’s earlier and suggests that important disease processes may start before visible plaque buildup.

mix_items.title: Galaxy Gallery: Galactic Gems Glisten in New Gallery From NASA’s Chandra
mix_items.summary: This gallery displays a collection of 16 galactic images from Chandra and other telescopes. Astronomers put galaxies into three main categories: spirals like our own Milky Way, ellipticals that are older and likely the results of mergers, and irregulars that can encompass a wide range of galactic phenomena. All types are represented in this collection. Each galactic image contains X-ray data from Chandra combined with data from telescopes such as NASA’s Webb, Hubble, IXPE, Swift, and NuSTAR, and others both in space and on the ground. The post Galaxy Gallery: Galactic Gems Glisten in New Gallery From NASA’s Chandra appeared first on NASA Science .

mix_items.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
mix_items.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

mix_items.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

mix_items.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
mix_items.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

mix_items.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
mix_items.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.
